questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.stem: A stye (hordeolum externum) is an acute infection of:
options: The gland of Zeis or Moll at the lid margin
questions.concept: An external hordeolum is a staphylococcal abscess of the lash follicle and its associated glands, treated with hot compresses, lash epilation and topical antibiotics. Internal hordeolum involves the meibomian gland.
questions.reference: AK Khurana Ophthalmology 8e, Diseases of the Eyelids

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.stem: A chalazion is:
options: A chronic non-infective lipogranuloma of the meibomian gland
questions.concept: Blocked meibomian secretion produces a painless firm nodule away from the lid margin. Incision and curettage from the conjunctival surface is standard; a recurrent chalazion in the elderly warrants biopsy to exclude sebaceous carcinoma.
questions.reference: AK Khurana Ophthalmology 8e, Diseases of the Eyelids

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.stem: Cobblestone giant papillae on the upper tarsal conjunctiva with itching in a young boy in summer indicates:
questions.concept: Vernal catarrh is a seasonal type I and IV hypersensitivity of young boys, with intense itching, ropy discharge, giant papillae and limbal Horner-Trantas dots. Mast cell stabilisers are the mainstay, steroids used sparingly.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.stem: Ophthalmia neonatorum occurring within the first 48 hours of life is most likely due to:
options: Chemical conjunctivitis from silver nitrate prophylaxis
questions.concept: Timing guides aetiology: chemical within 1 to 2 days, gonococcal at 2 to 5 days with hyperacute purulent discharge threatening corneal perforation, and chlamydial at 5 to 14 days. Gonococcal disease is a medical emergency.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.stem: A pterygium is:
options: A triangular fibrovascular growth of conjunctiva encroaching onto the cornea, usually nasally
questions.concept: Chronic ultraviolet and dust exposure drives pterygium formation, commonest nasally in the interpalpebral zone. Excision with conjunctival autograft has the lowest recurrence; a Stocker line of iron may mark its head.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.stem: Watering of the eye with regurgitation of mucopurulent material on pressing over the lacrimal sac indicates:
options: Chronic dacryocystitis with nasolacrimal duct block
questions.concept: A positive regurgitation test confirms sac distension proximal to a nasolacrimal duct block. This is a source of infection and an absolute contraindication to intraocular surgery until treated by dacryocystorhinostomy.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.stem: Congenital nasolacrimal duct obstruction in an infant is initially managed by:
options: Massage over the lacrimal sac with topical antibiotics, as most resolve by one year
questions.concept: Most membranous obstructions at the valve of Hasner open spontaneously; Criggler massage increases hydrostatic pressure to assist this. Probing is reserved for persistence beyond 9 to 12 months.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.stem: The Schirmer test measures:
options: Aqueous tear production, with less than 10 mm wetting in 5 minutes suggesting dry eye
questions.concept: Schirmer I without anaesthesia measures total secretion; tear film break-up time under 10 seconds assesses stability and indicates evaporative dry eye from meibomian gland dysfunction.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.stem: Entropion causing trichiasis is most importantly complicated by:
options: Corneal abrasion, ulceration and eventual opacity
questions.concept: Inturned lashes abrade the cornea causing recurrent ulceration and scarring, a major blinding mechanism in cicatricial trachoma - which is why lid surgery is the S of the WHO SAFE strategy.
questions.reference: AK Khurana Ophthalmology 8e, Diseases of the Eyelids

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.stem: Ptosis with a dilated pupil and the eye deviated down and out indicates:
options: Third cranial nerve palsy, requiring urgent exclusion of a posterior communicating artery aneurysm
questions.concept: Pupil-involving third nerve palsy suggests external compression, classically by an aneurysm, because parasympathetic fibres run superficially. Horner syndrome instead gives partial ptosis with a constricted pupil.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.stem: Acute anterior uveitis characteristically presents with:
options: Pain, photophobia, circumcorneal congestion and a small irregular pupil
questions.concept: Ciliary spasm causes pain and photophobia with ciliary injection, keratic precipitates, aqueous flare and cells, and posterior synechiae producing an irregular pupil. Cycloplegics and topical steroids are the mainstay.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.stem: Anterior uveitis is most strongly associated with which HLA type?
questions.concept: HLA-B27 associated acute anterior uveitis is typically unilateral, recurrent and alternating, occurring with ankylosing spondylitis, reactive arthritis, psoriatic arthritis and inflammatory bowel disease.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.stem: Mutton-fat keratic precipitates indicate:
options: Granulomatous uveitis, as in tuberculosis or sarcoidosis
questions.concept: Large greasy precipitates of epithelioid cells and macrophages on the corneal endothelium indicate granulomatous inflammation, prompting a search for tuberculosis, sarcoidosis, syphilis or leprosy.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.stem: Cycloplegics are used in anterior uveitis to:
options: Relieve ciliary spasm and prevent posterior synechiae
questions.concept: Atropine or homatropine rest the ciliary body relieving pain and keep the pupil dilated and mobile, preventing adhesions between iris and lens which would otherwise cause seclusio pupillae and secondary glaucoma.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.stem: Sympathetic ophthalmitis is:
options: Bilateral granulomatous panuveitis following penetrating injury to one eye
questions.concept: An autoimmune response to exposed uveal antigens after penetrating trauma or surgery threatens the uninjured sympathising eye, typically 2 weeks to 3 months later. Prompt enucleation of a blind injured eye within 10 days prevents it.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.stem: Scleritis is distinguished from episcleritis by:
options: Severe boring pain that disturbs sleep, with deep vessels not blanching on phenylephrine
questions.concept: Scleritis is intensely painful, may cause scleral thinning and perforation, and is strongly associated with rheumatoid arthritis and vasculitides, requiring systemic therapy. Episcleritis is mild and self-limiting.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.stem: Hypopyon uveitis with recurrent oral and genital ulceration suggests:
questions.concept: Behcet disease causes recurrent explosive non-granulomatous panuveitis with a mobile shifting hypopyon, retinal vasculitis, oral and genital aphthae, and pathergy. It requires systemic immunosuppression.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.stem: Endophthalmitis following cataract surgery most commonly presents:
options: Within a few days with pain, reduced vision and hypopyon
questions.concept: Acute postoperative endophthalmitis, usually from coagulase-negative staphylococci, is a sight-threatening emergency requiring urgent vitreous tap with intravitreal antibiotics. Delayed onset suggests Propionibacterium acnes.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.stem: Cytomegalovirus retinitis in advanced HIV appears as:
options: Pizza-pie fundus with haemorrhage and necrosis along vessels
questions.concept: CMV retinitis occurs at CD4 counts below 50, producing the characteristic brushfire or pizza-pie appearance of white necrosis with haemorrhage. Treatment is ganciclovir or valganciclovir with antiretroviral therapy.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.stem: Complications of chronic anterior uveitis include all EXCEPT:
questions.concept: Persistent inflammation causes complicated cataract, secondary glaucoma from synechiae, band keratopathy from calcium deposition and cyclitic membrane with hypotony. Pterygium is caused by ultraviolet exposure and is unrelated.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.topic: Retina & vitreous: vascular occlusions, ARMD, retinoblastoma
questions.stem: Sudden painless complete loss of vision with a cherry-red spot at the macula indicates:
questions.concept: The pale oedematous retina contrasts with the intact choroidal circulation at the fovea giving a cherry-red spot. It is an ocular emergency; irreversible damage occurs within about 90 minutes.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.topic: Retina & vitreous: vascular occlusions, ARMD, retinoblastoma
questions.stem: A blood-and-thunder fundus with flame haemorrhages in all quadrants indicates:
questions.concept: Venous obstruction causes widespread haemorrhages, dilated tortuous veins, cotton wool spots and disc oedema. The ischaemic type risks neovascular glaucoma at about 90 days - hence the term hundred-day glaucoma.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.topic: Retina & vitreous: vascular occlusions, ARMD, retinoblastoma
questions.stem: The hallmark of proliferative diabetic retinopathy is:
options: Neovascularisation of the disc or elsewhere
questions.concept: New vessels from retinal ischaemia bleed into the vitreous and cause tractional detachment. Panretinal photocoagulation and anti-VEGF therapy are the treatments; the earlier changes are non-proliferative.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.topic: Retina & vitreous: vascular occlusions, ARMD, retinoblastoma
questions.stem: Leucocoria in a child requires urgent exclusion of:
questions.concept: A white pupillary reflex, often with squint, is the commonest presentation of retinoblastoma, a life-threatening malignancy. Other causes include congenital cataract, Coats disease and persistent fetal vasculature.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.topic: Retina & vitreous: vascular occlusions, ARMD, retinoblastoma
questions.stem: Hereditary retinoblastoma is characterised by:
options: Bilateral multifocal tumours with germline RB1 mutation and risk of second malignancies
questions.concept: Germline RB1 mutation follows Knudson's two-hit model, causing earlier bilateral multifocal disease with a lifetime risk of osteosarcoma and other second cancers, so siblings and offspring require screening.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.topic: Retina & vitreous: vascular occlusions, ARMD, retinoblastoma
questions.stem: Age-related macular degeneration typically causes:
options: Progressive loss of central vision with preserved peripheral vision
questions.concept: Macular involvement destroys central acuity for reading and faces while navigational peripheral vision is retained. Dry ARMD shows drusen and atrophy; wet ARMD has choroidal neovascularisation treated with intravitreal anti-VEGF.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.topic: Retina & vitreous: vascular occlusions, ARMD, retinoblastoma
questions.stem: Retinitis pigmentosa classically presents with:
options: Night blindness with progressive constriction of visual fields and bone-spicule pigmentation
questions.concept: Rod degeneration causes nyctalopia and ring scotoma progressing to tunnel vision, with waxy disc pallor, attenuated arterioles and perivascular bone-spicule pigment, and an extinguished electroretinogram.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.topic: Retina & vitreous: vascular occlusions, ARMD, retinoblastoma
questions.stem: Rhegmatogenous retinal detachment is preceded by:
options: Photopsia and floaters from a retinal break, then a curtain over the visual field
questions.concept: A break allows liquefied vitreous under the neurosensory retina. Warning symptoms of flashes and sudden floaters warrant urgent examination, as prompt laser to a break prevents detachment. High myopia is a major risk factor.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.topic: Retina & vitreous: vascular occlusions, ARMD, retinoblastoma
questions.stem: Papilloedema is distinguished from papillitis by:
options: Preserved visual acuity in papilloedema despite a swollen disc
questions.concept: Papilloedema from raised intracranial pressure is bilateral with normal acuity, enlarged blind spot and no pain, whereas papillitis is usually unilateral with marked acuity loss, a relative afferent pupillary defect and pain on movement.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.topic: Retina & vitreous: vascular occlusions, ARMD, retinoblastoma
questions.stem: The commonest cause of vitreous haemorrhage in an adult in India is:
questions.concept: Bleeding from fragile new vessels in proliferative diabetic retinopathy causes sudden painless loss with loss of the red reflex. Ultrasound B-scan assesses the retina when the fundus cannot be seen.
